extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations; PR educators
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter recounting the historical development of public relations and articulating enduring principles, tactics, and ethical standards for PR practice. Useful as guidance for organizing, planning, and evaluating public relations programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of organized publicity drives
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized publicity and sales drives can rapidly mobilize public action and dramatically expand reach (example: Liberty Bonds holders grew from about 350,000 to 10 million within six months after two organized publicity and sales drives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coordinated, organized campaigns to raise funds, recruit participation, or shift public behavior; plan drives with clear calls to action and coordinated channels. The Liberty Bonds example serves as empirical evidence of scale effects from organized publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of grassroots advocacy and third‑party endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners (e.g., Carl Byoir) introduced grassroots advocacy groups and the third‑party endorsement as persuasive tactics to popularize products and causes (credited with popularizing the Jeep, tubeless tires, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate authentic‑appearing grassroots support and credible third‑party voices to lend legitimacy to messages. Examples: product campaigns, social causes; ensure endorsements are appropriate and credible to target audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as counsel / 'engineering public consent'
rubrics_metrics.description: Edward Bernays framed PR as 'engineering public consent' and promoted the role of the 'public relations counsel'—PR as strategic counsel to influence public opinion and build consent for policies or products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position PR practitioners as strategic advisors involved in planning and shaping organizational policy and public messaging rather than merely as press agents. Integrate research, messaging strategy, and audience psychology into counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and duty to inform (Arthur W. Page)
rubrics_metrics.description: Page: 'All business in a democratic country begins with public permission and exists by public approval... business should be cheerfully willing to tell the public what its policies are, what it is doing, and what it hopes to do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt transparency as a core principle: communicate policies, actions, and intentions proactively. Treat disclosure and explanation as a duty to maintain public approval and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public opinion polling to plan and evaluate programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Arthur W. Page was among the first to use the new science of public opinion polling as the basis for planning and evaluating public relations programs; Roper and Gallup polls (mid‑1930s) became respected tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate systematic measurement (polls, surveys, market research) to inform planning, test messages, and evaluate outcomes. Use reliable sampling and question design; treat measurement results as inputs to adjust programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibility of counsel to oppose harmful client policies (John W. Hill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hill: 'Should an existing client company adopt policies which the counsel believes are not in the public interest, he would advise against such policies—and, if he has integrity, be prepared to resign the account in case the client persisted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR counselors must advise against actions contrary to the public interest and be willing to disassociate from clients whose policies conflict with ethical obligations or public welfare. Maintain integrity over client retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer continuous, positive PR programs over occasional defensive efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Post‑Depression trend: movement away from occasional and defensive efforts toward more positive and continuous programs administered by established departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ongoing, proactive communication programs rather than episodic crisis responses; institutionalize PR functions to sustain relationships and preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of paid advertising as a public relations tool
rubrics_metrics.description: World War II expanded paid advertising's role in PR (public relations advertising, public service advertising, issue/advocacy advertising, institutional advertising); the War Advertising Council used advertising to mobilize wartime behaviors (produce, recycle, ration, buy bonds, serve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage paid media strategically as part of PR mixes—use public service and institutional ads to reach and persuade target publics. Coordinate advertising with earned and owned media for consistent messaging and calls to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical use of 'media blitz' in campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitaker–Baxter introduced the 'media blitz' in the final days of political campaigns as a potent tactic; even small budgets can succeed with decisive, concentrated media effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy intense, concentrated media activity at key moments to maximize visibility and influence; plan timing, message consistency, and channel saturation for blitz effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate market research and communication science
rubrics_metrics.description: Social scientists' postwar work contributed to market research, public opinion polls, and communication science—providing tools for more precise planning and assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate research methods and communication theory into campaign design (segmentation, message testing, media selection, evaluation). Build or consult research capability for evidence‑based PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary mission: forge relationships of understanding, trust, and respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Betsy Ann Plank: 'Public relations is fundamental to a democratic society... Its primary mission is to forge responsible relationships of understanding, trust and respect among groups and individuals—even though they often disagree.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orient PR goals toward building durable relationships, not solely short‑term persuasion. Prioritize credibility, listening, and dialogue as central activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as central tool in advocacy and protest strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil rights and protest movements used PR strategically—Dr. King: 'Public relations is a very necessary part of any protest or civil disobedience... [asking] for a hearing in the court of world opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PR to frame issues, raise awareness, and mobilize public opinion for advocacy causes. Ethical advocacy should aim to explain grievances, build sympathy, and seek public accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allowing messenger identity (e.g., gender) to overshadow ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Doris Fleischman: when ideas were considered first in terms of my sex, they might never get around to being judged on their own merits; she learned to withdraw where gender skewed reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure communications so ideas are evaluated on merit; be mindful of biases about messenger identity and, where necessary, reframe or disassociate message from gendered perceptions to ensure fair consideration.
